governance.context: A personal proof of concept on synthetic relational data, focused on PII classification and consistent pseudonymization.
governance.problem: Masking sensitive identifiers one field at a time can break joins, constraints and cross-system consistency. Moving unprotected data into development or analytics environments increases exposure.
governance.goal: Inventory and classify PII columns, apply consistent pseudonyms across related relational data and check that the protected dataset retains the intended technical properties.
governance.responsibility: I designed and documented the CLI workflow, classification and masking rules, protected-database checks and automated tests.
governance.architecture: The local workflow generates synthetic data, inventories schemas and relationships, profiles and classifies fields, applies pseudonymization rules and validates the protected schemas. YAML policies are versioned; value mappings remain in memory during a batch.

decisions.heading: Consistency across tables
decisions.text: Deterministic pseudonyms use an external key, normalization and namespaces. Approved technical keys stay stable to preserve relationships: records remain linkable, so the result is pseudonymized rather than anonymous.

decisions.heading: Ambiguous classifications
decisions.text: Ambiguous classifications require an explicit decision before masking. Manual review adds work but avoids applying an arbitrary rule.

results.label: Synthetic inventory
results.detail: 20 source and 20 protected tables; 109 columns inventoried and classified in the reference workload.

results.label: Documented checks
results.detail: The repository suite checks relationships, constraints, absence of schema drift and deterministic idempotence on the synthetic dataset.

governance.limits: The workflow has been tested on synthetic data. Use with real data would require evaluation of classification, operational key management and monitoring; pseudonymization alone does not establish legal compliance.
governance.diagram_note: From synthetic data generation to relationship checks.
governance.checks: The project suite tests counts, constraints, cross-table relationships, consistency groups, schema drift and deterministic idempotence on the synthetic workload.

dbt.context: A personal Data Engineering project built on synthetic e-commerce data.
dbt.problem: Late orders, subsequent corrections and columns introduced in later runs can create duplicates or inconsistent business metrics unless ingestion and transformations share explicit rules.
dbt.goal: Build repeatable loads, a dimensional model with an explicit grain and checks that make corrections and dashboard metrics verifiable.
dbt.responsibility: I built the data generator, raw ingestion, dbt models, tests and Streamlit dashboard. Business measures are defined and checked in the marts; the interface presents them without recalculating them.
dbt.architecture: Python generates reproducible CSVs and loads them into DuckDB with a transactional manifest. dbt organizes staging, current-version selection and dimensional marts. An order-line fact connects to customer, product and date dimensions; Streamlit reads a snapshot in read-only mode.

decisions.heading: Deterministic upsert
decisions.text: order_line_id is the stable key. The current version is selected by updated_at and, on a tie, a canonical payload comparison. This adds complexity but makes replay and arrival order irrelevant to the final state.

decisions.heading: Visible anomalies
decisions.text: Economically invalid rows remain in the fact but do not contribute to revenue. Missing dimension keys point to technical Unknown members, retaining the fact without claiming the data is complete.

results.label: Incremental load
results.detail: In the documented synthetic dataset, 10 new late rows and 5 corrections lead to 5,010 distinct order_line_id values, with no final duplicates.

results.label: Checks
results.detail: Documented tests show idempotent replay and parity between incremental and full-refresh results for the fact and dimensions.

dbt.limits: Tests cover a local synthetic workload. Real sources and larger volumes would require evaluation of runtime, monitoring and how the dashboard snapshot is refreshed.
dbt.diagram_note: Synthetic data; Streamlit reads the DuckDB snapshot in read-only mode.
dbt.checks: Project tests cover grain uniqueness, business rules, idempotent replay and parity between incremental and full-refresh results for the fact and dimensions.
dbt.visual_caption: Authentic Streamlit dashboard screenshot from the personal project, using synthetic data.

nosql.context: A group Data Engineering project developed during the ITS programme, using Databricks and Inside Airbnb data for Amsterdam and Rio de Janeiro.
nosql.problem: Organize listings and reviews from two cities while separating ingestion, transformation and analytical queries.
nosql.goal: Structure the data in Bronze, Silver and Gold layers to support analysis and comparisons between the two cities.
nosql.responsibility: I led the team and focused mainly on data ingestion, helping structure the Bronze layer. The Silver transformations, Gold queries and visualizations are presented as group work.
nosql.architecture: The Bronze notebook sets up ingestion from four detailed listings and reviews CSVs in a Databricks volume, adds city and ingestion timestamp, and includes definitions for four Delta tables. The Silver notebook brings Amsterdam and Rio listings into silver_listings with UNION ALL and converts selected types and prices. Gold contains SQL views and analytical queries; an export preserves two chart configurations.

decisions.heading: CSV ingestion
decisions.text: Bronze reads fields as strings and configures multiline input, quotes, escaping and PERMISSIVE mode for complex text. The project documentation explains the choice of detailed datasets to retain ratings.

decisions.heading: Layer separation
decisions.text: Silver combines listings with UNION ALL and prepares fields for analysis. Listing deduplication is outside the documented transformations.

decisions.heading: City-specific comparisons
decisions.text: Amsterdam and Rio use different currencies, so prices need to be compared within each city. Some Gold queries need a city filter to follow that rule.

results.label: Source notebooks
results.detail: The Bronze ingestion flow, silver_listings transformation and Gold analytical views and queries are documented.

results.label: Visualizations
results.detail: The export retains settings for two charts, one by city and one by accommodation type.

nosql.limits: This case presents the architecture defined in the notebooks. Reproducing the flow requires completing silver_reviews and correcting some Gold queries; quantitative results from a complete run are not documented.
nosql.diagram_note: The notebooks separate ingestion, listings transformation and SQL analysis.
nosql.checks: The code review covers Bronze definitions, silver_listings, Gold views and two chart configurations. Some queries need correction before a new run.
